title: The node's knowledge graph: agent memory on LightRAG
description: The node's agents keep what they learn and find it again by meaning. Knowledge outlives the conversation, and an agent reads a short extract instead of whole files.
keywords: knowledge graph, LightRAG, agent memory, graph RAG, Fractera node

blocks.title: Your agents stop forgetting what they learned
blocks.description: The graph keeps the knowledge of every element of your node: what was studied, how it connects and where it came from. Any agent finds what it needs with one question instead of rereading old files and conversations.

blocks.text: An element hands the graph what it learned: the things, the links between them and a short text saying where it came from.
New knowledge settles next to what is already known, and the same thing found in different analyses becomes one point.
For a question in plain words the graph returns a short context: the right things, their links and the source.
Only building costs tokens; reading calls no language model.

blocks.title: Without a shared memory every conversation starts from zero

blocks.text: An agent studied someone else's site, worked out how its cart works and explained it all to you. The conversation closed and the finding was gone. A week later another agent does the same work again, and you pay for the tokens again.

blocks.text: Picture a map where the towns are things and the roads are the links between them. A site, its search, the request address that search uses and the item of your quiz that grew out of it are points on that map, joined by labelled lines. The graph remembers both the points and the roads between them.

blocks.text: Only building costs much: a model reads the material and picks out the things and the links between them. Either LightRAG does it when it writes a document, or the element agent that has already studied the material hands the graph ready links. Reading is almost free: the question becomes an embedding, and the graph finds the nearest things and links and returns a short context without calling a language model. The agent passes the keywords for the graph search itself. You pay once to build and read many times for next to nothing.

blocks.between: One space never sees the points and roads of another.

blocks.text: The deep memory sends what each element was told into that element's graph space: memory for the main agent, memory-<element> for an element. The shared graph with the skills base and the studied products never sees a space, and a space never sees the shared graph.
A question of an element goes to its own space. The main agent's question goes to every space, and the contexts come together.
The spaces divide what the graph answers. Its doors open with the node's key, and the computer it runs on is yours.

The graph runs inside the node on your computer, and its data sits in the node's folder. Elements read it and add to it through the element's doors with the node's key. When you need to, you can connect your own tools to the same doors.

children.text: An agent works out how a feature of someone else's site is built and writes into the graph the site, the feature, the requests behind it and the quiz item that grew out of it. The finding does not vanish with the conversation.
Collections of skills, MCP servers and any set where it matters not only what is in it but how one thing relates to another. The graph keeps them in order and finds what you need by meaning.
The memory of all the node's agents

Everything that happened in the agents' lives in one place: what happened and when, which element, node and partner it involves, which event was the cause and which the effect. Together it gives the whole picture of your project.

blocks.text: Every element of the node already has the node key. Store what you learned as a ready graph and find it again with your own keywords:
The answer brings the entities, the links and the fragments they came from; when nothing relevant is there it says found: false. Add "space": "<name>" to keep a graph of your own.

head: Part
What it does
rows: LightRAG 1.5.7
Lives inside the element: Python managed by uv, one pinned package, installed into the element's own folder
One operation per call
Each call starts Python for one operation, about 2 seconds and 200 MB while it lasts, and runs take turns
No language model
The caller brings the graph and the keywords; the vectors are counted by the node's embeddings element, 384 numbers, no key
Spaces
space: "<name>" keeps a graph of its own in its own folder, and the shared graph never sees it
Origin
Knowledge of a studied product is marked external-study, so an agent never takes it for this node's code
The lock
The node key in X-Node-Key; the page «Knowledge graph» shows the architect its size and a search

items.q: Do I need to install anything?
items.a: No. The element installs Python and LightRAG into its own folder, and nothing goes into the system.
In the node's folder on your computer. The graph lives in the memory of its process, and the files on disk are its copy.

items.q: Can I connect to the graph from outside?
items.a: Yes. Today the node's elements use the graph through its doors with the node's key. You can connect your own tools to the same doors.
An open-source library for search over a knowledge graph, from the LightRAG Team under the MIT license. The node's graph is built on it.

items.q: What if the graph gets very large?
items.a: The built-in storage is enough for the knowledge of one node. A graph of millions of things needs a database server, and this element does not set one up.

blocks.text: Built by Fractera for the [Lagrix](https://lagrix.dev) protocol and for any web2 project whose agents need a shared memory. MIT license, the code is at [github.com/Fractera/fractera-graph-lightrag-starter](https://github.com/Fractera/fractera-graph-lightrag-starter).
